title: Fixing the AI Infra Scale Problem by Stuffing 1M Sandboxes in a Single Server
gist: Unikraft's CEO describes a cloud platform built on unikernel/microVM technology (Firecracker-based) that achieves ~10ms cold boots, stateful scale-to-zero, and demonstrated density of one million sandboxed VMs on a single server, arguing this solves the AI-agent-sandbox and headless-browser density problem that container and Kubernetes-based approaches cannot, while warning that agent credentials must never live inside the sandboxed VM itself.

themes.theme: Isolation primitives and the case for VMs over containers

insights.claim: The trusted computing base (TCB) — the pile of software all workloads share and depend on for security — is just the hypervisor for a VM (each VM gets its own OS and runtime), but is the entire host OS (tens of millions of lines of code) for containers, and the host OS plus the full language runtime for language-level isolates, making VMs the most isolated model by design even though nesting a container inside a VM looks inefficient.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: A rigorous security argument (smaller TCB = fewer vulnerabilities) for why VM-based isolation should be the default for untrusted or adversarial workloads like AI agents, not containers or language sandboxes.
insights.quote: Containers don't contain, isolates don't isolate, and so VMs are the golden standard in the cloud.
insights.locator: Let me ask you a question, what do you think

insights.claim: A microVM is defined purely by its VMM (virtual machine monitor) being a lightweight launcher like Firecracker rather than QEMU — a 16GB Ubuntu VM launched by Firecracker is still technically a microVM; a unikernel is a VM built with only the OS pieces a specific application needs and nothing else.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: Clarifies frequently confused industry terminology (microVM vs unikernel vs VM), useful for accurately evaluating vendor claims in the sandboxing/isolation space.
insights.locator: How many people have heard the term microVM?

insights.claim: ECS's approach of running containers inside VMs is a form of 'isolation within isolation' that trades efficiency for safety because containers alone are 'not safe enough' — the speaker's own opinionated take is that the container layer is unnecessary overhead and the application should be placed directly into a purpose-built VM instead.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: A direct architectural critique of AWS ECS's and Kata Containers' container-in-VM model from a competing infra vendor, relevant when evaluating container-platform security tradeoffs versus pure-VM/unikernel platforms.
insights.locator: That's what ECS, for instance, does

insights.claim: Unikraft's research lineage traces through ClickOS (10-20 Gbps software packet processing in a VM, published in an early paper) and a hot-take paper 'My VM is Lighter (and Safer) than your Container' that pushed 8,000 VMs onto a single server with millisecond cold-boot times and received about 28,000 citations, followed by a 'Unikraft: Fast, specialized unikernels the easy way' paper with about 8,000 citations, before becoming a Linux Foundation open-source project seven years ago.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: Establishes multi-year, peer-reviewed technical credibility (high citation counts) behind the density and boot-time claims made later in the talk, rather than these being unvalidated marketing numbers.
insights.quote: My VM is Lighter (and Safer) than your Container
insights.locator: Of course, we did a hot take white paper

insights.claim: When Unikraft first deployed its Dockerfile-to-VM CLI on AWS expecting the ~10ms cold boot achieved on local servers, they instead measured about 30 seconds, revealing that a cloud platform's actual latency is dominated by the load balancer, proxy, VM-lifecycle controller, and VMM chain surrounding the image — not the image itself — requiring the whole chain to be rebuilt for millisecond performance.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: A cautionary, quantified lesson (10ms expected vs 30s measured) for any infra team assuming a fast VM image alone delivers fast end-to-end latency — the whole platform stack (LB, proxy, controller, VMM) must be re-engineered.
insights.locator: Instead of 10 milliseconds, who wants to guess

insights.claim: Unikraft chose not to use QEMU (too slow/chunky) or Intel Cloud Hypervisor (caused CPU jitter and high idle CPU consumption when scaled to thousands of VMs) as its VMM, using Firecracker instead after benchmarking revealed the scheduler quality differences.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: A specific, benchmarked vendor comparison among VMM choices (Firecracker beats Intel Cloud Hypervisor and QEMU at scale) relevant to any team building high-density VM infrastructure.
insights.locator: If you know Intel Cloud Hypervisor, we didn't use

insights.claim: Snapshotting a VM's memory state lets applications with slow startup (e.g., 2-10 seconds, or a JVM) resume from a pre-initialized snapshot in about 10 milliseconds instead of re-running full startup, and the same snapshot mechanism enables forking (for creating sub-agents), checkpointing/rewinding to a sane state, and live migration between servers.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: Snapshot-based application masking is a generalizable technique that could be applied by any infra team to eliminate slow-starting-runtime penalties (notably JVM-based services) in serverless/sandbox contexts.
insights.locator: The idea is to use something called snapshots

insights.claim: Scaling to hundreds of thousands to a million scale-to-zero VMs on a single server broke standard Linux infrastructure assumptions: one TAP device per VM overwhelmed the kernel (freezing the kernel lock and breaking NTP/SSH/Tailscale), the Linux bridge port limit was hit, and IPv6 lock contention emerged, all requiring custom low-level Linux networking fixes.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: Documents specific, previously-undocumented Linux kernel scaling ceilings (TAP devices, bridge port limits, IPv6 lock contention) relevant to anyone attempting extreme-density VM deployments on stock Linux.
insights.locator: The Linux host was pretty upset that we were using

insights.claim: Measured cold-start times across 100,000 VMs held steady at about 10 milliseconds; the controller pre-sizes for a million VMs ahead of time using a few kilobytes of metadata per sleeping VM (about 12GB total), and full differential/compressed snapshot storage for a million VMs would require about 12 terabytes, feasible on standard servers with two 2TB NVMe drives (with room to add more).
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: Concrete quantified capacity-planning numbers (10ms at 100K VMs, 12GB controller memory, 12TB snapshot storage for 1M VMs) that make the million-VM-per-server claim independently checkable against commodity NVMe hardware costs.
insights.locator: A little bit in numbers. This is a graph

insights.claim: The live demo showed 1,024,132 scale-to-zero VMs running on a single server, with individual sandboxed Claude/OpenClaw agent instances resuming from sleep in real time to answer queries and then returning to a zero-resource standby state.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: A live, verifiable demonstration (not just a claimed benchmark) of over one million VMs on a single server, directly relevant to any AI-agent sandbox infrastructure vendor's density and cost claims.
insights.locator: Here I wanted to show you on the box.

themes.theme: Applications: AI agent sandboxes, headless browsers, Kubernetes integration

insights.claim: Headless browsers (usually Chromium), the workhorse for AI agents retrieving web content, take 30 seconds to a minute to start and consume 4-16GB of memory each, forcing teams to keep fleets running idle to stay reactive; scale-to-zero with ~10ms wake time removes the need to keep them running continuously, dramatically improving density.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, expensive infrastructure cost center for AI-agent companies (idle headless browser fleets consuming 4-16GB each) that scale-to-zero microVM tech can directly reduce — a concrete infra-cost optimization opportunity.
insights.locator: The problem with Chromium is it takes forever

insights.claim: Sandboxes for AI agents require strong isolation because agents are untrusted ('who trusts agents these days'), are used intermittently (idle periods interspersed with activity), and sandbox vendors need extreme scale — making scale-to-zero microVMs with fast resume and state retention specifically well-suited to the AI-agent sandbox use case.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: Directly frames Unikraft's product as purpose-built infrastructure for the AI-agent sandbox market, a fast-growing infra category as agentic AI products scale.
insights.quote: Obviously, you require strong isolation because who trusts agents these days.

insights.claim: Unikraft built a virtual kubelet that presents itself to Kubernetes as a normal node accepting pod scheduling, but under the hood schedules a Firecracker microVM instead of a container and always reports the pod as 'running' even while the VM is actually asleep — giving Kubernetes's self-healing, HA, and scalability benefits while retaining millisecond scale-to-zero semantics that Kubernetes itself cannot natively provide.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: A concrete integration pattern letting enterprises keep their existing Kubernetes tooling and workflows while gaining microVM-level density and speed — lowers the adoption barrier versus a rip-and-replace platform migration.
insights.locator: What we did is we built a virtual kubelet

insights.claim: The speaker states his team evaluated KubeVirt (Kubernetes' own VM approach) but found it slow, and after investigating what contributed to the slowness, decided building a custom virtual kubelet from scratch was cleaner than patching KubeVirt's codebase.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: A direct competitive critique of KubeVirt's performance from a company that built and shipped an alternative — relevant to teams evaluating VM-on-Kubernetes options.
insights.locator: We did do a lot of work in the past with KubeVirt

insights.claim: Even with strong VM-level isolation, an AI agent could still gain root access within its own kernel by exploiting the Linux user-space/kernel divide, but that root access would be confined to its own VM's kernel and could not affect other tenants' VMs.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: An honest limitation disclosure: VM isolation is strong for cross-tenant protection but does not prevent an agent from fully compromising its own sandbox — credential and secret placement policy still matters most.
insights.locator: First thing, it is possible that the bad agent

insights.claim: The speaker states current best practice is that sensitive credentials (e.g., an Anthropic API key or a credit card) should never live inside the agent's sandboxed VM itself; instead they should live in a host-side proxy with firewall rules that inject credentials into outbound requests, while the agent itself has no direct access to that proxy — noting this practice is evolving on a monthly basis.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable security architecture recommendation (credential-injecting host proxy, no direct agent access) for anyone deploying AI agents with API keys or payment credentials — directly relevant to reducing credential-exfiltration risk highlighted elsewhere in AI-agent security coverage.
insights.quote: Don't give your credit card to the agent. I can't believe people are doing this.
insights.locator: Then the second level is, yes, you should never

insights.claim: When demand exceeds a server's core count (e.g., 48 cores), the system either degrades performance (longer boot times, with teams setting an acceptable degradation threshold) or queues requests, or horizontally scales by spinning up additional stopped EC2 instances pointing to an AMI within about 15-20 seconds to absorb peak demand, then shutting them back down afterward.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: Describes a specific elastic-bursting mechanism (pre-staged stopped EC2 instances activated in 15-20 seconds) that lets a fixed-core server fleet absorb demand spikes without over-provisioning — a concrete cost-optimization pattern for cloud infra teams.

insights.claim: The speaker's overall takeaway is that cloud infrastructure historically forced a tradeoff of picking only two of speed, scale, and strong isolation, but with careful engineering all three can be achieved simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Felipe Huici
insights.so_what: A concise thesis statement framing Unikraft's core value proposition and implicitly the industry-wide unresolved tension it claims to have solved — useful shorthand for evaluating competing sandbox/microVM infra vendors against this three-way tradeoff.
insights.quote: In cloud infra, it used to be the case you have to pick speed or scale or strong isolation or two out of three.
